newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Greenpeace in new action against altered soybeans.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace in new action against altered soybeans.

text.p: Greenpeace activists, continuing a worldwide campaign, painted slogans against genetically modified soybeans on a grain ship on its way to the Belgian port of Antwerp, Belga news agency reported on Sunday.

The environmentalists, in inflatable dinghies, painted the slogans on the hull of Stanislaw Kulczynski late on Saturday while the ship was still on a river in Dutch waters in order to avoid heavy Belgian fines.

Greenpeace said on Friday that U.S. grain giant Cargill had taken out an injunction banning the environment pressure group from interfering with the arrival of the cargo, which Greenpeace describes as "contaminated" with genetically modified soybeans.
Greenpeace said it faced fines of a million francs ($32,000) an hour if it came within a km (half a mile) of the grain ship, which arrived in Antwerp later on Saturday night.
Greenpeace says genetically modified foods are untested and a potential environmental time-bomb.

A tiny portion of this year's soybean crop in United States has been produced from plants genetically altered to withstand a widely-used weedkiller. Washington insists there are no health risks and shippers have mixed altered beans and older varieties together.
The Greenpeace ship Sirius has already been impounded in Antwerp and faces a fine of $19,000 for interfering with the arrival of the Bunga Saga Empa with a cargo presumed to include altered soybeans.

Shortly before that it had called off another action against a Cargill shipment when the world's biggest privately owned grain company took out an injunction that also carried with it fines of $30,000 an hour for any breach.
The European Union has no full policy on genetically changed food, although it has approved the importation of some specific modifications.
On Thursday the European Parliament urged EU governments to segregate and specifically label modified soybeans.
On Friday, the U.S. government urged consumers on Thursday not to be swayed by "rhetoric and emotion."
Acknowledging European mistrust of the beans developed in the United States, Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman reminded consumers that most cancer drugs were based on similar science.
